content.title: Response to Reviewer ynap
content.comment:
Q1: Not first CLIP+DG, and weaker than DPL?

A1: I believe General Response has partially answered this question. We consider source-free DG as a trend for DG tasks. CLIP is used to bypass the need for source domain samples using diverse text descriptions, which is quite different from applying CLIP to DG tasks.

Our approach achieves close to DPL results without source domain data. In addition, our method achieves better performance than DPL on the new test domain in Table 4. As you can see, the performance of DPL on the test domain also differs when training with different source domains (e.g., for DPL [1], (P, A, S)-> X 91.9% and (P, C, S)-> X 96.0%), which validates your point that the use of source domain data introduces more bias.



Q2: Mean pooling is good enough? The performance improvement mainly benefits from CLIP?

A2:  I believe General Response has partially answered this question. We compared the performance difference between MP and CAE. CAE achieves considerable improvements over MP, which was verified on several datasets as well as multiple domains.

Besides,  t-SNE (see Figure 4) shows the effect of CAE visually. Since the distance metric in the aligned vision-text embedding space of CLIP is cosine similarity rather than L1 or L2 distance, reconstruction through cosine similarity can learn the common semantic representations (i.e., class-related semantic) from text description of different domains, which helps to form domain-unified representations.

content.title: Response to Reviewer eFx2
content.comment:
Q1: CLIP+DG can work, but not novel?

A1: I completely understand your concern and appreciate your taste in research. We believe this concern comes from our failure to articulate our motivation and thinking well. We elaborate further in General Response. This includes why source-free DG, how to bypass the dependence on images through text, and how to better extract domain-unified representations through CAE reconstruction. 



Q2: The results when directly using CLIP?

A2: Thank you for your suggestions, which have helped the integrity of the experiment. In the paper we compared the "empty prompt", which approximates the results of using CLIP directly. Further, we tested the standard CLIP (using the official 80 prompts provided for mean pooling) in the response to reviewer T6gD. As shown in Table A, our method has better performance.



Q3: Why we need source-free DG. Do we loss the the meaning of DG?

A3: We have elaborated on this in our general response. The second issue is very insightful and we would like to discuss it further with you.

We believe that source-free DG does not mean that the meaning of DG is lost. DG capability and DG task are two concepts. the DG capability is what we need, while the DG task is just a way to evaluate the DG capability. The current DG task that divides the source and target domains is just a compromise measure because we have no better way to directly and accurately measure DG capability. The source-free DG is also asking for the DG capability of the model and is somehow closer to the real scenario, where datasets separated by domains are not available. It is an expansion of the meaning of DG.



Q4: Some captions and fronts (e.g., the size)should be improved?

A4: Thank you for your suggestions, we have made adjustments in the new submission version. And we would appreciate it if you have more specific suggestions.



Q5: What about source-free domain adaption (DA)?

A5: Tasks involving domains derive many different settings because of the more informative data and labels. We will identify these tasks and discuss why we do not compare source-free DA. if you still have doubts, further discussion is welcome.

Let's start by identifying **DG & DA**. DG, as discussed in A3, DG is the capability of the model itself, while DG task is a way to test DG capability. Therefore, the DG task strictly requires that the target domain is unknown, because the target domain is only a simulation of unknown scenarios. While DA is essentially an engineering problem that can be categorized as transfer learning. The target domain is the real target scene of the task, so it is available in the training.

Thus, source-free takes on a very different meaning for DG and DA. For DG, source-free DG requires an unsupervised model with good DG capabilities. This is a generalization of the previous DG task. While for DA, source-free means that the data in the source domain is no longer available during migration learning, and it is a more challenging DA task. But it still aims at better performance on the target domain rather than testing the DG capability of the model.

content.title: Response to Reviewer UajX
content.comment:
Q1: Though the problem is new, the proposed method is based on the language prompt, which is not insightful enough?

A1: Thank you for recognizing that the research questions we ask are novel and interesting, which is essential to the study. Our approach is not complicated, but simple, effective, and requires less effort. We have detailed our design philosophy in General Response, which we hope will bring more inspiration. 



Q2: The domain bank is hard to cover all the domains in the open-world scenarios?

A2: This is an important issue as it relates to the choice of source domains in the domain generalization task. First of all, we would like to remind that it is a great benefit of our approach to have this as a choice.  It is almost impossible to cover the open-world scenario. For a normal DG task, the selection of each domain feature requires the collection and labeling of a large number of corresponding samples.  Narrowing down the needs of thousands of samples to a single textual description is one of our contributions to cope with the open-world scenarios.
Regarding how to choose domain banks, we show experiments in the manuscript (See Table 3), and the results show that "Combined "corresponds to the best results, and "Expanded" is better than "Task". Therefore, we also recommend using as diverse descriptions as possible in the case of unknown test scenarios. In fact, "Expanded"already contains most of the fields we can think of.

It is costly to provide a real open-world scenario dataset, and the DG task actually simulates open-world scenario by a small portion of unknown domains, and we collected data from two new domains to help this simulation as well. The results show a good performance of our method (See Table 4).



Q3: The motivation and strength of CAE? 

A3: Thank you for your suggestion, the intuition and motivation for CAE does deserve more elaboration, and we have further clarification in General Response. We will add more explanation in the revision.



Q4: Domain bank is strong prior and limits the scalability of the method?

A4: I believe our A2 has partially answered this question. the experimental setup of DG is exactly simulating the open-world scenario.
The reason for using the domains of the dataset as prompts is that these are the most common ones. Therefore, there is also a lot of duplication between several datasets.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Leveraging the capabilities of large-scale vision-language models this work presents a source-free method for learning robust prompts that perform well on the task of domain generalization. By using a domain bank and the class names for the task of interest, the authors present two methods for learning prompts which can generalize to many domains. Despite not requiring access to source samples to learn these domain unified prompt representations, the authors show that the results are competitive with domain generalization methods which take into account all of the source domain data. 

The Source-Free Domain Generalization setting that the authors propose is novel and challenging, however its unclear if it has useful applications as a method for combining it with labeled source samples is not discussed and it performs less well than approaches on similar backbones which incorporate source samples.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is clearly rewritten, straightforward to reproduce and provides a novel take on the task of domain generalization. The two proposed approaches are intuitive and provide insightful ways to think about prompt design. The results on the domain generalization challenges are strong, especially considering that no source data is used in this method. 

However, this work does not adequate compare itself with other methods of prompt learning. The most straightforward comparison would be using the proposed domain bank, and ensembling the results of various prompts as proposed in the original CLIP paper (Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision).
Other few-shot prompt learning approaches, such as CoOp (Learning to Prompt for Vision-Language Models), CoCoOP (Conditional Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models) would also be valid baseline to consider in this scenario. In essence this is a zero-shot learning approach and would be best compared with other few-shot or zero-shot learning approaches especially those which share the same backbones as its hard to distinguish how much of the increased performance comes from this approach versus the more robust CLIP backbones.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly presented, and has several novel components such as the CoSine AutoEncoder and the source-free domain generalization framing. The work should be straightforward to reproduce. More in-depth baseline comparison would improve the quality of the work.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work takes an interest approach to learning prompts for specific tasks. The is significant interest and capability in improving model performance through learning better language prompts and this work makes strides in this area. As of now, without a baseline to compare with a simple prompt ensembling approach it is hard to tell if the improvements observed are meaningful. More work should be done to position this work in regards to other prompt learning efforts.

Q1: Is it useful when source samples incorporated?  Performs less well than DPL?

A1: As elaborated in General Response. First, our method aims to achieve good DG capability without source domain data, which belongs to unsupervised learning. In addition, our method does not rely on source domain data and performs domain-unified representations at the text side, so it is not prone to introduce domain bias, which is well illustrated in Table 4. The performance of DPL is weaker than that of CAE for different source domain settings, and different source domain settings also affect the performance of DPL.

Q2: Compare to other prompt learning method, including few-shot prompt learning method?

content.title: General Response-1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive review of our manuscript. We were encouraged to hear that the reviewers found the source-free domain generalization (SFDG) to be interesting (Reviewers *UajX*) and that they view our methodology as novel and effective (Reviewer *T6gD*, *ynap*). 

We also noted several general concerns from reviewers that also touched on our key points. Therefore, we respond to them here in a unified manner.

We will also respond to questions raised by each reviewer individually.

Q1: Why source-free domain generalization?

A1: 

**Source-free DG implements the need for DG under the paradigm of unsupervised learning**. Before we start, we remind that DG is a capability of the model, and the DG task is a test of the model's DG capability. For tasks with limited data volume, enhancing their DG capability is a source-free DG  task. Now let's review the different DG task settings.

| Task             | Accessible                                           |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| multi-source DG  | sample: different domains, label: [domain, category] |
| single-source DG | sample: single domain, label: [category]             |
| source-free DG   | sample: **none**, label: [category]                  |

The ability to generalize to other domains is an essential property of a machine-learning model. It is not required only for supervised models. In the field of machine learning, data is precious. Unsupervised learning, and zero-shot learning are all designed to cope with some data deficit. Therefore, it is also necessary to improve the performance of unsupervised models, and source-free DG fills the blank.

In summary, DG is a capability of machine learning models, and it is equally important for supervised and unsupervised models. And our source-free DG fills the blank of DG for unsupervised models.

**Source-free DG is a more challenging task**. More source domain data usually leads to achieving better performance. For example, in the latest work, the SOTA multi-source domain generalization method [1] achieves much higher performance than the latest single-source domain generalization method [2] on PACS. In Table 4, existing DG methods get very different performance on the same target domain when the source domains are different (e.g., for DPL [1], (P, A, S)-> X 91.9% and (P, C, S)-> X 96.0%), which further shows that the source domain data will bring  bias to traditional DG task. We believe that when the number of source domains is limited, training on source domain data will introduce more or less domain-related biases. However, the current mainstream domain generalization datasets have only a small number of domains (e.g., PACS: 4 domains, DomainNet: 6 domains). Therefore, we propose source-free DG to avoid introducing the bias of source domain data, and try to extract domain-unified representations from the rich knowledge of vision-language models. Further, as shown in Table 4, our method achieves better performance than DPL [1] on two open-world source domains (i.e., pixelate and geometric) without training with any images, which further demonstrates the good generalization of our proposed method.

content.title: General Response-2
content.comment:
Q2: The proposed method is not insightful enough.

A2:

Compared to most DG methods, our approach is less complicated to implement. However, it does achieve better performance without relying on source domain data and consuming fewer computational resources. We are willing to share our design ideas further, which we hope will help to understand our approach.

To improve the DG capability, a straightforward idea is to train the model to find common features among different source domain samples. This is the reason why single-source DG is more difficult than multi-source DG. For example, L2D [4] allows the model to retain some features that are most likely to contribute to domain generalization throughdata augmentation. And for source-free DG, data augmentation does not work either.

**Why CLIP?** To avoid the problem of finding common features of different domain images, we transform the problem into finding common features of different domain languages through a vision-language model. Through such a detour, the cost of data acquisition is dramatically reduced while the efficiency of feature extraction is significantly improved. We consider this idea to be more enlightening than the specific details of the method. 

**Why CAE?** A good performance may also be achieved by directly mean pooling the representations generated by prompts for different domains. However, the distance metric in the aligned vision-text embedding space of CLIP is cosine similarity rather than L1 or L2 distance. That is to say,  the semantic similarity is calculated by cosine similarity, and directly taking the mean value is a crude approach. Therefore, we use CAE to first close the distance between different domain representations and expand the distance between different class representations by measuring the cosine similarity between the text embeddings, so that the generated domain-unified representation better preserves the features that are domain invariant and helpful for classification. Figure 4 and Section 4.4 offered an intuitive understanding. 

In general, our approach is designed to solve SFDG tasks, CLIP to treat the dependence on data in textual form, and CAE to obtain domain-unified representations.

[1] Zhang, X., Iwasawa, Y., Matsuo, Y., & Gu, S. S. (2021). Amortized Prompt: Lightweight Fine-Tuning for CLIP in Domain Generalization. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2111.12853*.

[2] Wan, C., Shen, X., Zhang, Y., Yin, Z., Tian, X., Gao, F., ... & Hua, X. S. (2022). Meta Convolutional Neural Networks for Single Domain Generalization. In *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition* (pp. 4682-4691).

[3] Radford, A., Kim, J. W., Hallacy, C., Ramesh, A., Goh, G., Agarwal, S., ... & Sutskever, I. (2021, July). Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 8748-8763). PMLR.

[4] Z. Wang, Y. Luo, R. Qiu, Z. Huang and M. Baktashmotlagh, "Learning to Diversify for Single Domain Generalization," *2021 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)*, 2021, pp. 814-823, doi: 10.1109/ICCV48922.2021.00087.
